body.text: Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae has been in the limelight since before President Lee Jae-myung became president in June 2025. These days, his name drapes over most news as the ruling Democratic Party (DP) resolved to impeach him during its general meeting on November 20.

“Despite Cho’s violation of the Constitution, we have been restraining ourselves while awaiting the public’s understanding. But now, we cannot further condone his attempt at justifying collaboration with insurrection and distorting history,” Kim Min-seok, the DP leader, said.

Accordingly, the party set up an impeachment task force, planning to submit Cho’s impeachment motion to the National Assembly (NA) in early December. There are a few grounds for the impeachment cited by the DP, but let’s consider three major ones here.

First, on the night of former President Yoon Suk-yeol’s failed self-coup on December 3, 2024, Cho idled by – legally and symbolically. As a bastion of constitutional rule of law and democracy, the Supreme Court failed to counteract Yoon’s unconstitutional declaration of martial law. Rather, the meeting presided over by Cho at the Supreme Court in the early morning hours of December 4, 2024, concluded that “the command and supervision of the judiciary transfers to the martial law commander.” The court decided to “prepare its future steps according to the martial law commander’s instructions and the martial law manual.”

The DP holds that, at a time when even those lacking legal knowledge immediately knew that Yoon’s martial law was unconstitutional in every sense, the Supreme Court reneged on its duty to uphold the constitutional rule of law and protect people’s right to life and property. Cho’s acquiescence to Yoon’s martial law feels all the more chilling in hindsight given how, as per the constitution, the Supreme Court is the final arbiter over court martial cases. It means that, had Yoon’s self-coup succeeded, the Supreme Court under Cho could have – not that it would have, because we would never know – provided legitimacy to Yoon’s martial law.

Second, Cho has been refusing to recommend a new candidate for a Supreme Court justice. Under the constitution, the chief justice recommends a candidate and the president appoints them. And the convention is for the former to coordinate with the latter in advance to agree on the candidate.

There has been an empty justice seat since March 2026, yet Cho delayed recommending a replacement until August. Even then, he did so without consulting President Lee Jae-myung. Former President Yoon packed the Supreme Court with right-leaning justices – eight out of 12 Supreme Court justices were appointed by him, in addition to Cho as chief justice. Lee rejected the recommendation for a more balanced composition, asking for another recommendation. Cho hasn’t budged.

The DP maintains that Cho’s unilateral decision infringes upon the president’s right to appoint personnel and that Cho abandoned his constitutional duty to make the Supreme Court whole for the people to receive fair trials.

On the other hand, Cho argued that “there’s no constitutional ground for the National Assembly and the president to interfere with the procedure for the chief justice’s recommendation.” He went so far as to describe the president’s behavior as “unconstitutional.” Of course, he’s entitled to his opinion, but it’s inappropriate for him to publicly express his personal constitutional interpretation. That’s entirely up to the Constitutional Court, whose sole job is to clear up any ambiguities in the constitution.

Plus, Cho’s public denouncement of the democratically elected president as “unconstitutional” seemed nothing more than the judiciary’s foray into the executive. (Remember that Cho had been thoroughly silent on Yoon’s declaration of martial law – which was palpably unconstitutional from the outset and hence ruled as unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court.) Despite the constitution’s lack of elaboration on the Supreme Court justice nomination, the convention of presidential-judicial consultation has come to reflect the original intention of constitutional legislators. The DP is calling Cho’s decision to snub this convention an example of “judicial elitism,” the judges’ sense of entitlement that they trump the other two branches of the government and the people’s sovereignty represented by elected officials.

The third rationale for impeachment is Cho’s track record of procedural impropriety in criminal justice. In May 2024, ahead of the June presidential snap election, Cho disregarded all procedural regularity and the Supreme Court’s regulations on judicial deliberation to expedite the case against Lee Jae-myung, then the DP’s presidential candidate and odds-on favorite to win the election. The Supreme Court rushed to overturn an appellate court verdict that found Lee innocent; a guilty verdict would have barred him from running for the June election. At the time, all the 10 justices who ruled against Lee were appointed by Yoon, and they did so within nine days, during which they purportedly read all the 70,000 pages of documentation.

For another instance, Cho ignored the special counsel legislation. The Supreme Court should rule on cases indicted by the special counsel within three months of the appellate judgment. Former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo received a 15-year sentence for having aided Yoon’s attempted insurrection at the Seoul High Court. The Supreme Court, however, missed the deadline of August 7 to review the conviction. Instead, it dragged the case until November 19, overturning it in the end to partially acquit him. Eight out of nine justices who supported his partial acquittal were appointed by Yoon or Han himself when the latter was acting president following Yoon’s impeachment.

However, concerns are rife over the DP’s decision to impeach Cho. First, it’s unclear whether Cho’s behaviors so far have been illegal – even if they are worthy to be frowned upon. If some of his actions are deemed to be illegal, the legal threshold for the Constitutional Court to uphold impeachment is that the illegality has to be “significant enough to warrant dismissal.” It will be hard for the DP to save face if the constitutional court rules in favor of Cho.

Second, Cho’s tenure as chief justice ends next June. Constitutional Court decisions can take up to six months. By then, Cho will be out anyway, regardless of the ruling. In this context, the impeachment motion can be seen to be unnecessary and even melodramatic.

Third, Cho’s impeachment could alienate centrists. Although the DP has put forward plausible grounds for impeachment, the crux of the matter – and the real reason – is that the party abhors the Supreme Court’s rulings. If the Supreme Court ruled in favor of Lee in 2024 and against Han in November, no talk of impeachment would have arisen, regardless of Cho’s procedural irregularity and unreasonable demeanor.

Those on the political left – those supportive of Lee and seething against Yoon’s failed self-coup – would surely like to see Cho gone sooner rather than later. Centrists, however, regard the impeachment as the ruling party’s browbeating of the judiciary and vitiating the judges’ capacity for independent trials. A poll on November 25 found that almost half of South Koreans were opposed to impeaching Cho, as opposed to 33 percent in favor.

The legal sector is bristling. The chairman of the national conference of judges wrote online on November 22 that “once the court rulings themselves become a reason for impeachment, the judge will put a feeler out to political reactions before writing down their verdict.” He then urged his fellow judges to “action” if the DP really passes Cho’s impeachment motion. The Korean Bar Association also worried that the DP’s proposed impeachment “risks encroaching upon the separation of powers and judicial independence.”

Meanwhile, the opposition People Power Party believes that the real reason for the DP’s impeachment of Cho is to pack the judiciary with left-leaning judges so that they could acquit Lee should his suspended trials resume.

Next February is the periodic personnel appointment of judges. Once the NA passes Cho’s impeachment motion, the chief justice is excluded from his post. The most senior Supreme Court justice after Cho would take the helm as acting chief justice until the Constitutional Court’s judgment. That would be Chun Dae-yup, a centrist justice appointed by liberal former President Moon Jae-in. One can expect that the acting chief justice might reshuffle the judicial hierarchy in ways more palatable to the Lee administration. Jang Dong-hyuk, the PPP leader, scoffed on social media that this impeachment motion would pave the way for “President Lee’s jailbreak.”

Seo Young-kyo, the chair of the NA’s legislation and judiciary committee, is adamant. “There’s no such thing as the judicial branch’s independence under our constitution. The judiciary is subject to the legislature’s checks and impeachment if it behaves wrongly,” she said. Indeed, it’s the individual judges’ and their trials’ independence from external influences that the constitution safeguards, not the judicial branch itself as one of the state’s governing arms. If Chief Justice Cho tainted the judicial branch through procedural tweaking and public engagement to influence political outcomes, the judiciary should face due reaction from the legislature.

But one thing is clear. At a time when almost half of South Koreans distrust the judicial branch; when a chief justice can get away with meddling in public elections; when some judges still believe themselves to be above the law and popular sovereignty; and when a significant portion of the population still refuses to accept that Yoon’s martial law was unconstitutional and amounted to a short-lived self-coup, the public opinion over Cho’s impeachment will remain fractured and continue to fracture.
